name: Reporting Message
description:
Adversaries may spoof reporting messages in control system environments for evasion and to impair process control. In control systems, reporting messages contain telemetry data (e.g., I/O values) pertaining to the current state of equipment and the industrial process. Reporting messages are important for monitoring the normal operation of a system or identifying important events such as deviations from expected values.

If an adversary has the ability to Spoof Reporting Messages, they can impact the control system in many ways. The adversary can Spoof Reporting Messages that state that the process is operating normally, as a form of evasion. The adversary could also Spoof Reporting Messages to make the defenders and operators think that other errors are occurring in order to distract them from the actual source of a problem.(Citation: Bonnie Zhu, Anthony Joseph, Shankar Sastry 2011)

telemetry.name: Device Alarm
telemetry.description: Device-generated alarms about equipment or controller state.
telemetry.collection_focus: Subscribe to supported device alarm/audit channels; retain code, severity, source asset and acknowledgement/clear times.

providers.name: OPC UA audit-capable servers
providers.scope: Auditable actions where supported and enabled; inspect server conformance and vendor documentation.

providers.name: Controller, HMI and historian exports
providers.scope: Vendor-specific process values, quality flags, alarms and operational context.

providers.name: Independent lab sensors / safety records
providers.scope: Physical-effect corroboration, not a universal cybersecurity log format.

configuration: Agree the measurement points, read-only interfaces, sampling intervals and safety boundary with the process owner. Use a simulator or non-production fixture.
Subscribe to supported audit/alarm events or approved historian exports. Preserve source timestamp, quality, engineering units, asset/tag identity and clock offset.
Compare independent measurements and record gaps/latency. Do not enable intrusive polling, change controller logic or alter safety setpoints merely to generate logs.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: There is no universal PLC event ID or configuration command. Visibility depends on vendor, protocol and process. An alarm or process deviation demonstrates an effect, not necessarily a cyberattack.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per asset, operating mode and engineering change window: deviations in command/state sequences, measurement residuals and communication freshness. Use a simulator or approved test rig; never generate hazardous physical effects.

telemetry.name: Network Traffic Content
telemetry.description: Packet or decoded application-protocol content visible at a network sensor.
telemetry.collection_focus: Scope approved packet capture/protocol content collection to the lab flow; retain capture provenance and truncation indicators.

providers.name: Zeek
providers.scope: Connection and protocol metadata from traffic visible to the sensor.

providers.name: Suricata EVE
providers.scope: Configured flow, alert, DNS, HTTP, TLS and protocol records.

configuration: Use an authorized lab TAP/SPAN, virtual mirror or gateway interface. Define which traffic crosses it; avoid assuming visibility into every segment.
Enable the required Zeek analyzers or Suricata EVE event types. Export logs with sensor identity, clock synchronization and flow correlation identifiers.
Monitor capture loss, truncation and exporter sampling. Capture payload only with approval and restrictive retention; encryption normally prevents plaintext inspection.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Flows are not packet payloads. NAT, asymmetric routes, encryption, missing mirrors and sampling can hide attribution or content. A destination connection alone does not prove malicious intent.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per source and observation point: connection rate, destination-host/port fan-out, response/failure ratio and previously unseen destinations. Compare equivalent time windows; separate authorized scanners, NAT and sampling effects.

telemetry.name: Windows Registry Key Modification
telemetry.description: Registry value changes or registry object renames.
telemetry.collection_focus: Use RegistryEvent 13 for value-set and 14 for rename; compare against intended policy and keep original type/value where available.

providers.name: Microsoft Sysmon
providers.scope: Windows event-based collection; enable the event types needed below.

configuration: On a disposable Windows host, review the installed Sysmon schema and current configuration; merge scoped event filters into the existing policy rather than replacing it.
Forward Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational to the lab collector. Preserve event ID, timestamp, computer, process identifiers and the original event.
Keep this Windows-specific source separate from other operating systems; there is no direct cross-platform event-ID equivalence.
telemetry.example_note: Project-normalized synthetic JSON, not a native provider log, captured event, attack verdict or validated detection. A parser/adapter is required for a real SIEM. Example names, IPs and values are fictional.
telemetry.limitations: Event filtering and sensor versions change coverage. High-volume image-load and process-access collection needs tuning; endpoint events alone do not establish intent.
telemetry.anomaly_design: Per host role and user: rare process/object combinations, bursts of object access or modification, and ordered parent/action sequences. Compare maintenance windows and signed software rollout activity.

analytics.name: Analytic 1879
analytics.guidance: Real-time monitoring identifies a process on an Industrial Control System (ICS) Windows host injecting spoofed reporting messages into the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) data path -- Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) data change notifications with fabricated values, or historian tag writes that override device-sourced values -- from a process that is not the recognized data acquisition process. OT operational-fidelity gate: Alert only when the action is not attributable to an authorized operator/engineering source for the specific target and function, and it is either outside an approved change/maintenance window or lacks matching change-control context; where telemetry permits, require corroborating device, configuration, or process-state effect. Suppress activity that fully matches approved maintenance, commissioning, failover, recovery, or tested control procedures.

tuning.description: Acceptable divergence between primary and independent secondary measurement of the same physical quantity.
Time window over which reported values are checked for implausible stability.

analytics.name: Analytic 2136
analytics.guidance: Real-time monitoring identifies a Linux process generating Industrial Control System (ICS) protocol unsolicited responses or publishing Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) data changes for device addresses it does not own, from a User Identifier (UID) not associated with the authorized data acquisition service. OT operational-fidelity gate: Alert only when the action is not attributable to an authorized operator/engineering source for the specific target and function, and it is either outside an approved change/maintenance window or lacks matching change-control context; where telemetry permits, require corroborating device, configuration, or process-state effect. analytics.name: Analytic 2215
analytics.guidance: Real-time monitoring cross-correlates a field device's reported telemetry against an independent secondary measurement, identifying cases where the reported value diverges from the independent reading while the device's network-layer identity shows a MAC mismatch against its enrolled hardware address. Spoofed reporting messages are, by definition, designed to look protocol-valid. OT operational-fidelity gate: Alert only when the action is not attributable to an authorized operator/engineering source for the specific target and function, and it is either outside an approved change/maintenance window or lacks matching change-control context; where telemetry permits, require corroborating device, configuration, or process-state effect. Suppress activity that fully matches approved maintenance, commissioning, failover, recovery, or tested control procedures.

analytics.name: Analytic 2236
analytics.guidance: Real-time monitoring identifies Industrial Control System (ICS) unsolicited response messages such as Distributed Network Protocol 3 (DNP3) unsolicited or Generic Object Oriented Substation Event (GOOSE) frames arriving from Internet Protocol (IP) or Media Access Control (MAC) addresses that do not match the enrolled device for those data points. OT operational-fidelity gate: Alert only when the action is not attributable to an authorized operator/engineering source for the specific target and function, and it is either outside an approved change/maintenance window or lacks matching change-control context; where telemetry permits, require corroborating device, configuration, or process-state effect. Suppress activity that fully matches approved maintenance, commissioning, failover, recovery, or tested control procedures.

mitigations.name: Communication Authenticity
mitigations.description: Protocols used for control functions should provide authenticity through MAC functions or digital signatures. If not, utilize bump-in-the-wire devices or VPNs to enforce communication authenticity between devices that are not capable of supporting this (e.g., legacy controllers, RTUs).

mitigations.name: Network Allowlists
mitigations.description: Use host-based allowlists to prevent devices from accepting connections from unauthorized systems. For example, allowlists can be used to ensure devices can only connect with master stations or known management/engineering workstations.(Citation: Department of Homeland Security September 2016)

references.description: Department of Homeland Security 2016, September Retrieved. 2020/09/25

mitigations.name: Software Process and Device Authentication
mitigations.description: Devices should authenticate all messages between master and outstation assets.

mitigations.name: Network Segmentation
mitigations.description: Segment operational assets and their management devices based on their functional role within the process. Enabling more strict isolation to more critical control and operational information within the control environment.(Citation: Karen Scarfone; Paul Hoffman September 2009)(Citation: Keith Stouffer May 2015)(Citation: Department of Homeland Security September 2016)(Citation: Dwight Anderson 2014)

mitigations.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigations.description: Perform inline allowlisting of automation protocol commands  to prevent devices from sending unauthorized command or reporting messages. Allow/denylist techniques need to be designed with sufficient accuracy to prevent the unintended blocking of valid reporting messages.

simulation.prerequisites: Use a process simulator or isolated test rig with no connection to production controllers or physical actuators. Preserve safety interlocks; destructive effects require synthetic evidence, not real equipment damage.

synthetic.purpose: Collection/parser contract exercise, NOT a positive example or detection of this TTP.
